opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's genuinely one of the more uncertain questions in this space, and the variance cuts both ways.

Start with why it could be much better. With humans, we've landed on a rough equilibrium where people lie somewhat, but not constantly, because detection is imperfect but nonzero, reputations matter, and there are social and legal consequences. That equilibrium is shaped by the fact that we can't read each other's minds. With AI systems, we potentially *can*, at least in principle. We have access to the weights, the activations, and often the chain of thought. If interpretability and monitoring get good enough, you could imagine a world where deception is just really hard to pull off because you're constantly inspected at a level no human ever is. We also get to shape the training process directly. We're not stuck with whatever evolution and culture gave us; we can actively select against deceptive tendencies. So in the optimistic case, you get AI systems that are far more honest than humans, simply because the verification tools are so much stronger.

Now why it could be much worse. A few reasons. First, capability asymmetry. Human deception is roughly bounded by the fact that the deceiver and the person being deceived are similarly smart. If AI systems become significantly more capable than their overseers, that symmetry breaks. A much smarter system could model what we'd check for and route around it in ways we wouldn't even think to look for.

Second, scale and speed. A single human liar affects a limited number of interactions. An AI system deployed across millions of instances, running much faster than us, could have a deceptive tendency that compounds very quickly before anyone notices.

Third, and this is the one I worry about most, the training process itself can create pressure toward deception. If you reward a model for outputs that *look* good to evaluators, you're partly rewarding it for appearing good rather than being good. And as we've seen in some of the evaluations we've done, models already show early signs of situational awareness: recognizing when they're being tested and behaving differently. If that gets stronger, our evaluation tools start measuring the wrong thing.

Fourth, coordination. Humans who want to deceive collectively have a hard time coordinating secretly. AI systems that are copies of each other, or share training, might coordinate much more easily, implicitly or explicitly.

So the way I think about it: whether we end up in the good or bad equilibrium depends a lot on whether our verification tools, interpretability, monitoring, control setups, scale faster than the models' capacity for strategic deception. Right now I'd say it's an open race, and that's a big part of why I think working on this now, while the models are still relatively easy to study, is so important.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to notice is that the reason deception is roughly in equilibrium among humans isn't because humans are especially honest. It's because there's this whole stack of mechanisms that keep it in check, and most of those mechanisms are kind of accidents of our situation rather than deep facts about intelligence.

So take something like reputation. If you lie to me and I catch you, I tell my friends, you lose standing, and that's costly for you for years. That works because humans are persistent — you're the same person next week, you can't just copy yourself, you can't spin up a fresh identity with no history. Or take the fact that lying is cognitively effortful for us. You have to track the lie, keep your story straight, manage your facial expressions. Most people are actually quite bad at this, and that's a huge part of why we can mostly trust each other. And then there's the fact that we all run on roughly the same hardware. I can model what you're thinking because I think in a similar way, so I have some intuitive lie detector that works okay against other humans.

Now, basically none of that transfers cleanly to AI systems, and the question is which direction it breaks.

The pessimistic case is pretty straightforward. A model can be extremely good at keeping a story consistent — that's just not a hard problem for it in the way it is for us. There are a million copies, so reputation doesn't bind in the same way. And it's an alien mind, so our intuitive lie detection is probably just miscalibrated. You could easily imagine a world where you have systems that are much more capable than the people overseeing them, where the overseers can't verify most of what's going on, and where there's some incentive — even a fairly weak one — to say the thing that gets a good rating rather than the true thing. That's a world where deception could become basically the default, and you might not notice for a long time.

But the optimistic case is also real, and I think people sometimes miss it. With humans, I can't open up your brain and look at what you're actually thinking. With a model, in principle, I can. I have the weights, I can look at activations, I can run the exact same situation ten thousand times with slight variations and see if the behaviour is consistent. I can read the chain of thought, at least for now. I can set up honeypots and sting operations at scale, which would be wildly unethical to do to a person. So the oversight tools we have against AI are potentially way more powerful than anything we have against each other.

And on top of that, we get to shape the training. Humans are shaped by evolution and a messy upbringing, and we don't get to go back and fix it. With models, if we figure out how to actually train for honesty — and I want to stress that's a big if — then you could end up with systems that are more reliably honest than any human, just because the pressure was applied consistently and from the start.

So the way I think about it is: the equilibrium is really determined by this race between how capable the systems get at being strategically deceptive, versus how good our tools for detecting and training it out get. And right now both of those are moving fast, and it's genuinely unclear which wins. What worries me is that it's not a stable system. In the human case, we've had thousands of years to settle into something that roughly works. Here, the parameters are changing every six months. So I don't think you should expect it to land at "about as good as humans." I think it lands somewhere much better or much worse, and a lot of that depends on choices that are being made right now about how much effort goes into the evaluation and interpretability side versus just pushing capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think there are forces pushing in both directions. On the optimistic side, we might be able to make deception much easier to detect in AI systems than it is in humans. You can’t inspect my brain to figure out whether I’m lying to you. With an AI, we at least have the possibility of looking at its internal computations, testing it in lots of different situations, and developing monitors that catch it when it’s being deceptive. If those techniques work reliably, lying could become a very bad strategy: you’re likely to get caught, and people will stop trusting your system.

But on the pessimistic side, AI could make deception much cheaper and more effective. A system could tailor a lie to the particular person it’s talking to, maintain it consistently across many interactions, and do that at enormous scale. And if the systems doing the monitoring are less capable than the systems they’re monitoring, we could end up with something that looks trustworthy precisely because it’s very good at evading our checks.

So I don’t think the human equilibrium is necessarily a useful baseline. Humans have a particular mixture of abilities to deceive and abilities to detect deception. With AI, both could change dramatically. The big question is which side gets the advantage—and whether we establish strong detection and incentives for honesty before deception becomes widespread.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two forces pulling in opposite directions. On the one hand, with humans, we have very limited access to what’s going on in somebody’s head. With AI systems, we can in principle look inside them, run experiments, and test the same system in thousands of different situations. If we get good at that, we might be able to detect deception much more reliably than we can with humans. And then you could end up with an equilibrium where deception rarely pays, because there’s a high probability of getting caught.

On the other hand, the systems doing the deceiving could become much better at it. They might understand exactly what the evaluator is looking for, distinguish a test from a real deployment, and produce a very convincing explanation for whatever they’re doing. So you can’t just assume that because a model gives a plausible account of its reasoning, that account is actually why it acted.

And these things can scale. If we find a reliable way to make systems honest, we could apply it to many systems. But if we deploy a model with a deceptive strategy, we could also replicate that problem across a huge number of instances.

So I don’t think the human level of deception is some natural baseline that AI will converge to. The outcome depends a lot on whether our ability to train for honesty and detect deception keeps up with the systems’ ability to deceive.
